fields.meta_title: Advance Directive Form: Contents and Signing | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What goes in an advance directive form and how to sign it, plus a guided form that checks the agent and keeps each signed copy.
fields.h1: Build an Advance Directive Form in Plain Language
fields.hero_description: An advance directive form records the care someone wants if they cannot speak, and who decides for them. Describe who fills it in, and Emergent builds the form.
fields.features_heading: Where a Printed Directive Falls Short
fields.features_subheading: A healthcare directive form on paper sits in a drawer. Emergent's version asks plainly and files the signed copy.
fields.feature_1:
Each treatment as its own choice

Lists CPR, breathing machines, tube feeding and dialysis as separate questions, each answered yes, no or "my agent decides". Nobody is pushed into a choice they never weighed.
fields.feature_2:
An agent plus two alternates

Asks for the health care agent first, then two alternates in order, each with a phone number and a relationship. When the agent cannot be reached, the record shows who to call next.
fields.feature_3:
A signature page for your state

Prints the signature page with the witness lines or notary block named in your prompt. The person's choices fill the earlier pages, leaving a packet ready to sign in ink.
fields.feature_4:
Old directives read into fields

Reads an uploaded photo or PDF of a directive signed years ago and pulls out the agent's name and the date it was signed. Any field it cannot read clearly goes to a person.
fields.feature_5:
Every directive in a table you own

Saves each directive and every revision as a row in a database you own. Staff search by name and open the newest version, while earlier versions stay attached to the same record.
fields.feature_6:
The whole app exported as code

Exports the full code to your GitHub repo. An engineer can connect it to your records system through its API, or you can describe the change in a prompt and let Emergent write it.

fields.usecase_heading: Where Advance Directives Get Filled In
fields.tab_content_1:
Every adult patient asked at admission

Federal rules make Medicare hospitals inform adult patients about advance directives at admission and note in the chart whether one exists. Registration asks the question on a tablet. A yes asks for a photo or PDF of the document. A no sends a request to social work, and the answer is saved to the patient's record.
fields.tab_content_2:
When a witness turns out to be the agent

Clients rarely know that California bars the health care agent from signing as a witness. The intake questionnaire collects the agent and two alternates, then the witnesses the client plans to bring. If a witness name matches the agent, the draft is held and the attorney gets an email before anyone books the signing.
fields.tab_content_3:
Overdue reviews sent to one nurse

Wishes change after a new diagnosis or a move to memory care. Each resident's directive sits in one table with the number of months since its last review. Anything older than 12 months reaches the director of nursing as a Slack direct message, with the resident's name and the agent to call.
fields.tab_content_4:
A treatment decision on each screen

Most people stall partway through a printed packet. On a phone, the form asks about CPR, then breathing machines, then tube feeding, with "my agent decides" offered every time. A summary reads every choice back in plain words, and the packet prints with the signature page for their state.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an Advance Directive Form
fields.howto_description: The legal wording comes from the state. Your work is turning it into questions people can answer, then making sure the signed copy reaches the people who will need it.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Turn each treatment into a question
fields.howto_step_1_des: Find the official form for the state where the person lives and paste its sections into your prompt. Keep the statutory wording on the signature page, and rewrite only the instructions around each question into plain English.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put the health care agent at the top, then up to two alternates in order. Collect a phone number and relationship for each. Add a line asking the person to talk with their agent before naming them.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask about CPR, mechanical ventilation, tube feeding and dialysis one at a time. Describe each treatment in a sentence before the choice. Offer "my agent decides" alongside yes and no, and allow a different answer for permanent unconsciousness.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Add a free-text box for what the checkboxes miss: religious wishes, where they want to be cared for, how they weigh comfort against time. Agents lean on this section when a situation arises that the form never named.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Print the witness or notary requirements on the last page. In California, two adult witnesses or a notary will do, but the agent cannot witness, and at least one must be unrelated and inherit nothing from the person.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send a signed copy to the agent, each alternate and the person's doctor. Ask the hospital they use to add it to their chart. Record who received each copy and when. After any change, that list shows which copies to replace.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Set a reminder for every 12 months, and another after a new diagnosis or the death of the named agent. A review that changes an answer creates a new version and marks the old copies as replaced.

plan.angle: The top 10 is state PDFs, printable packets and explainers that hand a person pages of legal wording and stop there. This page says what the form holds (a living will and the appointment of a health care agent), how signing works in a state like California and where copies belong, then builds what a PDF cannot: one plain question per screen, a check that the agent is not also a witness, and one record of every directive a hospital, law firm or care community holds.

claims_to_source: The two most common advance directives are the living will and the durable power of attorney for health care; copies go to the proxy, health care providers and lawyer, papers in a safe deposit box need copies at home, and some states run registries
A living will records choices about treatments such as CPR, mechanical ventilation, tube feeding and dialysis
A POLST is a medical order filled out by a health care professional for people who are seriously ill or frail, while an advance directive is filled out by the individual
Hospitals in Medicare give adult patients written information about advance directives at admission and document in the record whether one has been executed
In California, an advance health care directive is signed before two adult witnesses or a notary, and the agent cannot act as a witness
In California, an agent must decide in line with the principal's instructions and known wishes
Advance directives fail in practice through vague language, problems with the proxy and copies that cannot be found
Barriers to completing an advance directive include discomfort talking about death, poor timing and too little information
